title: Lay-led communities
hookLine: independent minyanim, where members lead prayer themselves

lines: A WOMAN IN A SWEATER LEADS.
cards: A woman in a sweater gets up from a folding chair and begins the morning prayers. It's a rented room above a bookshop.
A borrowed Torah scroll waits in a cabinet, beside a box of prayer books someone carried up the stairs. There's no rabbi on a stage, because there is no stage.
Later a teenager reads from the Torah, nervous, carefully prepared. A retired dentist gives a five-minute thought on the week's portion. Next week, three different people will do those jobs.
Groups like this go by a plain name: an independent minyan.

teach.b: Lay-led communities. Four turns. First, the quorum.
A minyan is the group Jewish law asks for when a community prays together; the Mishnah lists prayers that are not said with fewer than ten. Streams differ on who counts toward the ten.
What the law asks for is people, not a building and not a title.
Second, the leader is a role, not a rank: the shaliach tzibbur, the messenger of the congregation. Jewish law does not require a rabbi for that job.
Any member who knows the prayers can carry the room's words for a while, then sit back down. Third, the old picture behind it.
At Sinai, the Torah says, God told the whole people: "ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation." Readers hear many things in that line.
Some in lay-led groups hear a job description: the holiness belongs to everyone in the room, so the work can too. Fourth, the cost. Nobody is paid to do it, so somebody has to.
Someone sets up the chairs, someone learns to chant a Torah portion, someone brings the food and stays to wash the cups.

Independent minyanim vary a great deal: some egalitarian, some traditional, some in between. Some members also belong to a synagogue with a rabbi, and value both. What they share is the habit of handing the work around.
A room like that exists because ordinary people decided to lead it.

how: In independent minyanim, members take turns leading prayer, reading from the Torah and giving short teachings, and members share the practical work of setting up, hosting and cleaning up.

o: a congregation ruled by an elected lay board

games.q: your small group wants to pray together, but there's no rabbi and no budget. what do you do?
o: wait until you can hire someone.
hand the jobs around: members lead, read and teach.
games.why: that is what independent minyanim do: the law asks for people, not a title, so members take turns leading.

practice: Think of a group you already belong to: a household, a team, a few friends.

Find one small job in it that usually waits for someone else, like starting the meal, picking the song, or opening a conversation that keeps getting postponed, and picture yourself doing it simply, without a speech.
If you pray, offer the job up as you breathe; if not, just hold the picture steady.

wordCard.voice: Lay-led communities. Groups where members, not paid clergy, lead prayer, read Torah and teach, taking turns as the messenger of the congregation. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: messenger of the congregation, the person who leads the prayers.

carryVoice: Your line: lay-led. The room's words can be carried by anyone who knows them. Until tomorrow.
